patients.summary: Retired postal worker in his 80s with hypertension, CKD 3b, hyperlipidemia, BPH and a remote stroke who joins in 2020. Course brings volume overload, a febrile rash illness with negative HIV testing, gout flares, E. coli prostatitis, syncope from severe aortic stenosis (he declines TAVR) and Listeria meningitis in 2026.

Filed to chart for PCP review before the new patient visit.

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
80 y/o man here to set up primary care. Retired from the postal service after a long career carrying mail. Lives in his own home in Southampton; his daughter is nearby and drove him today.

PMH (per patient and faxed records): HTN for decades; CKD stage 3b followed by his old PCP; hyperlipidemia; BPH, no troublesome urinary symptoms and never took a prostate pill; ischemic stroke years back, made a full recovery, no weakness or speech problems left over.
PSH: none.
Meds: lisinopril 20, amlodipine 5, HCTZ 25, atorvastatin 40, aspirin 81. Brought bottles, all match. Takes them with breakfast except the statin at night.
Allergies: NKDA.
FH: father had coronary disease; mother had high blood pressure and a stroke; a brother has type 2 diabetes.
SH: never smoked, no alcohol. Walks his street most days.

ROS: feels well. Denies chest pain, SOB, leg swelling, urinary trouble, new weakness.

Exam: Pleasant, sharp historian. Vitals in flowsheet. HEENT unremarkable. Neck supple. Heart regular, normal S1/S2. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender. Ext without edema. Neuro: strength and gait normal, speech fluent.

A/P:
1. HTN: reasonable today on three agents. Continue.
2. CKD 3b: last Cr in old records ~1.8. Repeat CMP, UA. Avoid NSAIDs, reviewed.
3. Hyperlipidemia / prior stroke: continue atorvastatin 40 and aspirin. Lipids today.
4. BPH: asymptomatic, no treatment.
5. Health maintenance: colonoscopy done at 71, normal, not repeating at his age. Tdap 2016. Flu shot when available in the fall. Will talk shingles and pneumonia vaccines next visit.

RTC 4 months, sooner prn. Can reach us by phone or portal any time.

documents.body: Mr. Robinson, your labs from yesterday are back. Kidney function is right where your old office had it, potassium is fine, and your cholesterol is well controlled on the atorvastatin. Exam: L 1st MTP red, warm, swollen, exquisitely tender, ROM limited by pain. Rest of foot fine, no skin break, no lymphangitic streaking.

A/P: Acute monoarticular podagra in a man on HCTZ with CKD. Clinical gout flare.
- Colchicine 0.6 mg once daily until it settles, max a week. Kept low given his kidneys. No NSAIDs (CKD).
- Ice, elevate.
- Message me in a few days; if not clearly better, will tap the joint.
- Talked about what gout is and things that can set it off.

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: tired, not hungry, ankles puffy.

HPI: 82M with HTN and CKD 3b. Since about the start of winter, roughly 4 months, he has felt more and more run down, eats less than he used to, and has noticed his ankles swell by evening. Lost about 4 lb without trying. Now and then a little lightheaded when he gets up from a chair, passes in seconds. No chest pain, no trouble breathing, no change in how he urinates. No fevers.

Meds unchanged: lisinopril 20, amlodipine 5, HCTZ 25, atorvastatin 40, ASA 81. NKDA. No NSAIDs.
SH: no tobacco, no alcohol.

Exam: BP 152/88, HR 72, BMI 26. Alert, conversant. Fundi: mild AV nicking both eyes. Neck: no JVD. Heart and lungs unremarkable. Abdomen benign. Trace edema at both ankles. Neuro grossly normal.

A/P:
1. Fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, edema in CKD 3b: concern kidney function has slipped with fluid retention. CBC, BMP, UA and urine protein/creatinine today. Renal ultrasound. Cut salt, aim under 2 g sodium a day, handout given and reviewed with daughter.
2. Volume overload on CKD: as above; will refer to nephrology for co-management.
3. HTN: above goal today; leave regimen for now until labs back, the lightheadedness argues against adding more.
4. Lightheadedness: brief, positional. Rise slowly.
I'll call him with results. RTC ~2 months.

documents.title: Results call
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Called pt (daughter on speaker). Reviewed: Hgb 11.5, Cr 2.1 (up from ~1.8 baseline), BUN 38. UA with 1+ protein, no blood, sediment bland. UPCR 0.3. Explained kidneys are working less well than last year and some fluid is hanging on. Ultrasound next week is set. Nephrology referral sent. Continue salt restriction; weigh himself a few mornings a week. Both voiced understanding.

reports.text:
EXAM: Ultrasound, kidneys and bladder.
INDICATION: Chronic kidney disease with edema.
COMPARISON: None.
FINDINGS: Right kidney 9.4 cm in length. Left kidney 9.4 cm in length. Both kidneys show increased cortical echogenicity relative to the liver and spleen. No hydronephrosis. No renal calculus or solid mass. Urinary bladder is unremarkable.
reports.conclusion: Bilaterally echogenic kidneys measuring approximately 9.4 cm, consistent with medical renal disease. No hydronephrosis.

documents.title: Nephrology Consultation
documents.author: nephrology
documents.body:
OUTPATIENT NEPHROLOGY CONSULTATION
Date of service: 05/23/2022
Referred by: primary care physician, for CKD stage 3b with edema.

Thank you for asking us to see Mr. Robinson, an 82-year-old gentleman with long-standing hypertension. Over the winter he had fatigue, poorer appetite, mild ankle swelling and a few pounds of weight loss. Creatinine 2.1 and BUN 38 on 4/18/22, up from about 1.8. Urinalysis 1+ protein with a bland sediment and no hematuria; protein/creatinine ratio 0.3. Hemoglobin 11.5. Renal ultrasound: echogenic kidneys about 9.4 cm bilaterally without hydronephrosis.

Medications: lisinopril 20 mg, amlodipine 5 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, aspirin 81 mg daily.
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: BP 138/80. No JVD. Lungs clear. Trace ankle edema, less than at his April visit per patient since cutting salt.

Impression: CKD stage 3b with low-grade proteinuria and mild volume overload. Small echogenic kidneys and a bland sediment point to chronic disease. A kidney biopsy would not change management and carries real risk with kidneys this size; not recommended.

Recommendations:
1. Continue current antihypertensives at present doses.
2. Sodium restriction under 2 g/day; he is already doing well with it.
3. Avoid NSAIDs and IV contrast where possible; renally dose new medications.
4. BMP every 3 to 4 months through primary care.
5. We will see him yearly, sooner if creatinine rises above 2.5.

Outpatient nephrology

documents.title: Same-day Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: sore throat, fever, rash.

HPI: 82M with CKD 3b, seen in April for fluid retention which has since settled. For 5 days: fevers at home, sore throat, aching muscles, tired, mild headache, and a blotchy rash on his chest and both arms. Not itchy. No new medications, no new soaps. No cough, no urinary symptoms. No stiff neck, no confusion, no light sensitivity.

Risk history: when I asked about HIV risk he told me, with some hesitation, that he injected drugs as a young man, decades ago, and has not used since. Never been tested that he knows of. No recent sexual partners.

Exam: afebrile here (took nothing today). Throat red, no exudate, tonsils not enlarged. Tender anterior cervical nodes both sides. Faint pink maculopapular rash scattered over chest and upper arms, blanching, palms and soles spared, no mucosal lesions. Neck supple, no meningismus. Heart regular. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, no spleen felt.

Point of care: rapid strep negative. Monospot negative.

A/P:
1. Febrile illness with pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy and rash: most likely viral. Given the remote injection history and that he has never been screened, HIV antigen/antibody today; hep C antibody added while drawing.
2. History of IV drug use, remote: added to the history.
3. Supportive care: fluids, acetaminophen as needed, no ibuprofen with his kidneys.
Call me if worse, new stiff neck, confusion, or rash blistering. I'll call with HIV and hep C results.

documents.title: Your test results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Mr. Robinson, both blood tests from yesterday came back negative: no HIV and no hepatitis C. That is good news. Keep resting and drinking fluids. I'll give you a call next Monday to see how the throat and rash are doing.

documents.title: Same-day Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Pt called at 8 am; seen late morning.

HPI: Two days of burning with urination, going far more often, and an ache between the scrotum and rectum. Felt feverish and shaky last night. No flank pain, no blood in urine, no vomiting. Known BPH, untreated.

Exam: uncomfortable but not toxic. Abdomen soft, no suprapubic or CVA tenderness. Gentle rectal exam: prostate warm, swollen and tender; no massage done.
UA dip: LE positive, nitrite positive. Culture sent.

A/P: Acute bacterial prostatitis.
- Ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 4 weeks; eGFR ~30, at the edge, this dose is acceptable. Discussed tendon and dizziness precautions.
- Fluids, acetaminophen for pain/fever.
- Urology referral given BPH.
- If unable to void, rigors, or not better in 48 h, ED. Will call with culture.

documents.title: Culture result
documents.author: RN

documents.title: Urology Consultation
documents.author: urology
documents.body:
UROLOGY CLINIC NOTE
Visit date: December 11, 2023
Reason: acute bacterial prostatitis, referred by primary care.

History: 83-year-old man with BPH, CKD 3b and hypertension, started on ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily on 11/20 for fever, dysuria, frequency and perineal pain; urine culture E. coli sensitive to ciprofloxacin. Three weeks in, no fevers, urinary symptoms nearly gone, stream adequate, no retention.

Medications: lisinopril, amlodipine, hydrochlorothiazide, atorvastatin, aspirin 81, ciprofloxacin.
Allergies: no known drug allergies.

Exam: afebrile, comfortable. Abdomen soft, bladder not palpable. DRE: enlarged, smooth, now nontender prostate without nodules.

Assessment: acute bacterial prostatitis, resolving. Benign prostatic hyperplasia, without bothersome symptoms at this time.

Plan: complete the full 4-week course. Repeat urinalysis after the course through primary care. No BPH medication needed now. Follow up with us as needed for recurrent infection or voiding trouble.

Outpatient urology

documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: R big toe.

HPI: Three days ago woke in the night with sudden pain in the right big toe; over the following two days it got steadily worse and now he can hardly walk on it. Had a similar flare in the left foot two years ago that settled on colchicine. Finished his ciprofloxacin course this morning for the November prostatitis; urinary symptoms gone. No fever, no injury.

Exam: R 1st MTP markedly tender, hot and red, with restricted range of motion. No open skin, no tracking redness up the foot.

Procedure: after verbal consent, skin prepped with chlorhexidine, dorsal approach to the R 1st MTP with a 22-gauge needle; small volume of cloudy yellow fluid aspirated. Tolerated well, bandage applied. Sent for crystals, Gram stain, culture.

A/P: Acute monoarthritis R 1st MTP, recurrent podagra; with recent infection, wanted to exclude a septic joint.
- Colchicine 0.6 mg daily up to a week, as last time.
- Will call with fluid results tonight; culture final in a few days.
- Ice, rest, elevate. Return immediately for fever or spreading redness.

reports.text: Sinus rhythm, rate 72. Voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy. No acute ST elevation.
reports.conclusion: Sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy.

reports.text:
Indication: syncope with exertion, systolic murmur.
Left ventricle: normal size with concentric left ventricular hypertrophy. Ejection fraction 60%. No regional wall motion abnormality.
Aortic valve: thickened and calcified leaflets with severely restricted opening. Peak velocity 4.4 m/s. Mean gradient 46 mmHg. Aortic valve area 0.7 cm2 by continuity equation.
Mitral, tricuspid and pulmonic valves: structurally normal.
Right ventricle normal size and function. No pericardial effusion.
reports.conclusion: Severe aortic stenosis (AVA 0.7 cm2, mean gradient 46 mmHg, peak velocity 4.4 m/s). Concentric LVH with normal LV systolic function, EF 60%.

documents.title: Emergency Department Record and Observation Discharge
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
REGIONAL HOSPITAL EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT / OBSERVATION UNIT
Arrival 04/02/2025 14:40. Discharged 04/03/2025 15:30.

Chief complaint: passed out on stairs.

HPI: 85-year-old man with CKD and hypertension, treated in 2022 for fluid overload, brought in by his daughter. While climbing a single flight of stairs at her house he went down; she reports he was out for only a few seconds and was back to himself quickly. He admits that for a few months he has tired more easily and gets a tightness in his chest when he exerts himself, easing with rest; he had not mentioned it to anyone. No palpitations beforehand, no tongue biting or incontinence, no head strike.

PMH: hypertension, CKD 3b, hyperlipidemia, BPH, gout, remote ischemic stroke without deficits, remote IV drug use.
Meds: lisinopril 20, amlodipine 5, hydrochlorothiazide 25, atorvastatin 40, aspirin 81.
Allergies: NKDA.
Social: never smoker, no alcohol.

Exam: BP 118/72, HR 72 regular, RR 16. Pale and tired-looking but alert and oriented. Carotid pulses weak and late-peaking. Harsh systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border carrying to both carotids. Lungs clear. No edema. No focal neurologic findings. No injuries.

ECG: sinus rhythm, LVH by voltage.
Labs: creatinine at his known baseline, potassium normal, hemoglobin in his usual low-11 range, WBC normal.
Echo (observation, 4/3): severe aortic stenosis, AVA 0.7 cm2, mean gradient 46 mmHg, peak velocity 4.4 m/s; concentric LVH; EF 60%.
Telemetry overnight: sinus rhythm, no arrhythmia.

Impression: exertional syncope and exertional chest tightness due to severe aortic stenosis.

Disposition: discharged home with daughter. Avoid strenuous activity and heavy lifting until seen by cardiology; sit or lie down if lightheaded. Medications unchanged. Cardiology clinic referral placed; follow up with PCP within one week.
Return for any further fainting, chest pain at rest, or breathlessness.

documents.title: Cardiology Consultation
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE CARDIOLOGY GROUP - CONSULTATION
Date seen: 4/23/2025
Referral: primary care and ED, severe aortic stenosis.

Mr. Robinson is 85 with hypertension, CKD 3b, hyperlipidemia and remote stroke. On 4/2 he had syncope climbing stairs, preceded by months of exertional chest tightness and fatigue. Echo 4/3: severe calcific aortic stenosis, AVA 0.7 cm2, mean gradient 46 mmHg, Vmax 4.4 m/s, EF 60%, concentric LVH. ECG: sinus, LVH.

Current medications: lisinopril 20 mg, amlodipine 5 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, aspirin 81 mg.
Allergies: none known.

Exam: BP 130/74, HR 70. Late-peaking harsh systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids, soft A2. Lungs clear. No edema.

Impression: severe symptomatic aortic stenosis (syncope, angina). Class I indication for valve replacement. Given age and CKD, transcatheter replacement is the natural option to evaluate.

Plan:
- Referral to the structural heart program for TAVR evaluation.
- Avoid heavy exertion; no driving pending evaluation.
- Continue current medications for now.

Thank you for the referral.
Cardiology

documents.title: Structural Heart Clinic
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
STRUCTURAL HEART CLINIC
Visit: 5/21/2025. Patient seen with his daughter.

Severe symptomatic aortic stenosis (syncope 4/2/25; exertional chest tightness). Echo: AVA 0.7 cm2, mean gradient 46 mmHg, Vmax 4.4 m/s, LVEF 60%.

He is independent at home, cognitively intact, and walks on level ground without difficulty. CKD 3b would require careful contrast planning for the pre-procedure imaging.

Assessment: reasonable TAVR candidate. We reviewed what the workup and procedure involve, the expected benefits for symptoms and survival, and the risks including stroke, bleeding, pacemaker need, vascular injury and kidney injury from contrast. We also discussed continuing with medical follow-up alone.

He would like time to think about this with his daughter before deciding whether to start the workup. He will let us know through his cardiologist or PCP.

Structural Heart Program

documents.title: Annual Wellness Visit with Advance Care Planning
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
AWV + ACP, daughter present for the whole visit.

Interval: structural heart clinic 5/21 found him a reasonable TAVR candidate. No further fainting; he keeps to one floor and walks slowly on flat ground. Mild chest tightness only if he hurries.

Functional: ADLs independent; daughter now does heavy shopping. No falls since April. PHQ-2 1 (a little down about the heart news, not depressed). Recall 3/3.

Advance care planning (35 min): We went through what the heart team told him and his own goals. He values staying in his home, being clear-headed, and not spending time in hospitals. He understands that without valve replacement the valve problem is likely to shorten his life and may cause more fainting or heart failure, and that the procedure could ease symptoms and extend life but has risks. After talking it through with his daughter over the past weeks, his decision is not to go ahead with valve replacement for now and to continue follow-up with cardiology; he knows he can change his mind. Health care proxy signed today naming his daughter. Full code for now; he wants to think more about resuscitation.

Exam: harsh systolic murmur radiating to the carotids, unchanged. Lungs clear. No edema.

A/P:
1. Severe AS: patient choice of medical follow-up; I will let cardiology know. Return precautions reviewed.
2. HTN/CKD 3b: labs today, meds unchanged.
3. Prevention: vaccines current; flu in fall.
RTC 3 months.

Plan: continue current medications. Avoid exertion and dehydration; stand up slowly. Clinic visits every 6 months. He knows the door to TAVR evaluation stays open if he changes his mind. Call for syncope, rest chest pain, breathlessness or swelling.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
REGIONAL HOSPITAL - DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted: 04/01/2026 (via ED to neuro ICU). Discharged: 04/10/2026 to short-term rehabilitation.

Principal diagnosis: Listeria monocytogenes meningitis.
Other active problems: severe aortic stenosis (medical management by patient choice), CKD stage 3b, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, BPH, gout, history of ischemic stroke without deficit.

Presentation: Three days of steadily worsening confusion and sleepiness. His daughter, who brought him in, said he had not been himself and seemed weaker after a family dinner; he had complained of mild belly cramps the day before. No fall or head injury, no sick contacts. Last hospital contact was the April 2025 ED visit for syncope.

Arrival: T 38.5 C, BP 138/76, HR 94, RR 18. Disoriented to date and place. Mild neck stiffness, light hurt his eyes. Moved all limbs symmetrically without focal weakness. Fundi normal. Abdomen soft and nontender.

CT head: age-related atrophy, no bleed.
Lumbar puncture: opening pressure elevated; fluid cloudy; WBC 1200/uL, 90% neutrophils; protein 210 mg/dL; glucose 25 mg/dL. CSF culture grew Listeria monocytogenes on day 3.

Course: Empiric vancomycin, ceftriaxone and ampicillin with dexamethasone were started after the LP. When Listeria was identified, vancomycin, ceftriaxone and dexamethasone were stopped and ampicillin continued alone, dosed for his kidney function. Mentation improved over 4 to 5 days; transferred to the floor on hospital day 4; oriented and at his cognitive baseline per daughter by discharge. Creatinine stayed at his known baseline. Home antihypertensives held the first two days, then resumed. PICC placed 4/8.

Discharge medications: ampicillin 2 g IV every 8 hours through 4/22/2026 (21 days total); lisinopril 20 mg daily; amlodipine 5 mg daily; hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily; atorvastatin 40 mg daily; aspirin 81 mg daily.
Allergies: NKDA.

Follow-up: PCP within 1 to 2 weeks of leaving rehab; PICC removal at completion of antibiotics; cardiology as scheduled.

Hospital medicine / neurology

SHORT-TERM REHABILITATION FACILITY - DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 4/10/2026 from the regional hospital. Discharged home 4/24/2026 with his daughter.

Reason for stay: completion of IV ampicillin for Listeria meningitis and reconditioning.

Course: Ampicillin 2 g IV every 8 hours completed 4/22 (21 days). No fevers. Remained oriented and conversant throughout. PICC removed intact 4/22. Worked with physical therapy daily; walking household distances independently at discharge and managing his own medications with his pill organizer.

Discharge medications: lisinopril 20 mg, amlodipine 5 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, aspirin 81 mg, all daily.
Allergies: none known.

Follow-up: primary care within one week.

documents.title: Transitional Care Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Post-discharge visit; daughter with him. Hospital summary (4/1-4/10) and rehab summary (4/10-4/24) reviewed.

Listeria meningitis: CSF WBC 1200 (90% PMN), protein 210, glucose 25, culture Listeria. Completed 21 days IV ampicillin 4/22, PICC out. Home since 4/24. No fever, no headache, no neck pain. Daughter says he is 'back to himself': follows the news, does his pills, joking with her. A bit deconditioned; weight down a few pounds from the hospital stay.

Med reconciliation: same five home medications, no antibiotics now. Matches rehab list.

Exam: alert, oriented x3, conversant. Neck supple. Murmur of AS unchanged. Lungs clear. No edema. Gait slow but steady without device.

A/P:
1. Listeria meningitis, treated: clinically recovered. Labs today.
2. Severe AS: no new symptoms; cardiology in July.
3. CKD 3b/HTN: BMP. Meds unchanged.
4. Deconditioning: home exercises from rehab, walk daily on level ground.
RTC early June.

Exam: alert, oriented. Neck supple. Systolic murmur unchanged. Lungs clear. No edema. Gait steady.

A/P:
1. Recovered from Listeria meningitis.
2. Severe AS, medical follow-up by his choice; cardiology July.
3. HTN/CKD 3b: labs today. Same medications.
4. Annual wellness visit and fall vaccines due; booking September.
RTC September.
